essence: Melania is a city whose square stages one endless comedy: its people are born into fixed stock roles and die out of them, so the dialogue never stops while every speaker is replaced, and the plot keeps edging toward a denouement that no single lifetime is long enough to notice.
textDetails: Whenever you step into Melania's square you are caught up in a dialogue that is already under way.
The braggart soldier and the parasite come out of a door and run into the young wastrel and the prostitute.
Or else the miserly father, from his threshold, delivers final warnings to his amorous daughter and is cut short by the foolish servant, who is on his way to take a note to the procuress.

Coming back after years, you find the same dialogue continuing: the parasite, the procuress and the miserly father have died, their places taken by the braggart soldier, the amorous daughter and the foolish servant, who have in turn been replaced by the hypocrite, the confidante and the astrologer.
The population renews itself: the participants die one at a time while their successors are being born, some into one role and some into another.
When someone changes role, abandons the square for good, or enters it for the first time, a chain of changes follows until all the roles are filled again.

Through it all the angry old man goes on answering the witty maidservant, the usurer goes on chasing the disinherited youth, and the nurse goes on consoling the stepdaughter, though none of them has the same eyes and voice as in the previous scene.
Sometimes one person plays two or more roles at once: tyrant, benefactor, messenger.

Sometimes a role is doubled and multiplied, given to a hundred or a thousand inhabitants: three thousand play the hypocrite, thirty thousand the sponger, and a hundred thousand are king's sons fallen into low estate, waiting to be recognised.
With time even the roles stop being exactly what they were.
Carried on through intrigues and surprises, the action heads toward some final denouement, which it keeps nearing even as the plot grows more tangled and the obstacles more numerous.
Looking into the square at successive moments you can hear the dialogue change from act to act; the inhabitants live too briefly to notice.
The text describes no architecture beyond the square, a door and a threshold. Design note, not stated in the text: the cast are the stock types of Roman comedy and the commedia dell'arte.
visualConcept: Melania is built as a Renaissance stage set floating in the dusk: a raised circular square is the stage, backed by a horseshoe of tall, flat, painted-looking house facades whose five openings lead into steep forced-perspective street vistas, like the receding streets behind the stage of the Teatro Olimpico in Vicenza. On the square, seventeen stock characters stand on chalk stage-marks, each identified by a costume colour and a small, softly glowing commedia mask; the masks are the permanent part of the city and the bodies wearing them are temporary. Actors visibly age, grey out and crumble to dust, the mask lifting off and hanging in the air over the empty mark, while newborns step out of the doors, grow as they cross the paving and receive it, and the dialogue never pauses: at a glance you see roles outliving people. Gold speech-beads shuttle between paired speakers, and above the square a single gold thread, the plot, coils into an ever denser knot around a small white star, the denouement it keeps approaching and never reaches. On the open south side the stage drops in shallow steps where the multiplied roles wait in their thousands: a field of ragged figures with tiny gold crowns, the king's sons fallen into low estate, awaiting recognition. The base is a disc plinth of warm travertine on an inverted cone of layered rock, with a row of footlights along the lip of the stage.
layout: Plinth: disc radius 21, top at y 0, rim 1.0 thick, underside an inverted rock cone 7 deep with strata. Stage-square: circle radius 8.5 raised to y 0.35, paved in concentric bands, a small well-head at the centre (r 0.6, h 0.5). Backdrop: a horseshoe of 11 tall houses on the northern 220 degrees of the rim (azimuth -110 to +110, north = 0), set at r 8.8 to 11.5, each 2.4-2.8 wide and 3.6-6.2 tall in three storeys, flat facades with an arched door (0.55 x 1.0) on a stone threshold step, one balcony, shutters. Five street openings in the horseshoe at azimuths -80, -40, 0, 40, 80, each 1.6 wide, running out to r 20 with the street floor rising 0.8 (raked like a stage); each lined on both sides by 6 houses shrinking from 1.0x to 0.4x scale with distance (forced perspective). South arc (azimuth 110 to 250): 6 concentric shallow terraces stepping down from the stage lip (y 0.35) to y -1.5 at r 18, each 0.3 high and 1.5 deep; 60 footlights (warm emissive beads with tiny reflector hoods) along the stage lip. Cast: 17 role-marks (chalk rings r 0.3) at radius 2.5-6.5 in five groups: NE soldier, parasite, wastrel and prostitute by a door; N miserly father on his threshold with the amorous daughter, the foolish servant crossing west with a white note toward the procuress at her door; E angry old man and witty maidservant; S usurer chasing the disinherited youth round the well; W nurse and stepdaughter; plus hypocrite, confidante and astrologer wandering between groups. Costume key: soldier crimson and gold plume, parasite olive, wastrel peacock blue, prostitute rose, miser black and red, daughter pale pink, servant harlequin lozenges, procuress violet, old man brown, maidservant blue and white, usurer bottle green, youth faded ochre, nurse white, stepdaughter grey-blue, hypocrite half grey half white, confidante lilac, astrologer midnight blue with gold stars. Multitudes at 1:100 of the text's numbers: 1000 king's sons kneeling or seated on the south terraces facing the stage (each with a gold crown glint), 300 spongers clustered round tavern tables in the five street mouths, 30 hypocrites with two-faced masks scattered among them. Plot-knot volume: sphere of radius 4 centred at (0, 10, 0), the denouement star at (0, 11, 0).
signatureMotion: 1) Succession: every 6-10 s one actor on the stage ages (costume desaturates to ash grey over 3 s, posture stoops 15 percent, gait slows), halts and crumbles into a small puff of grey dust that sinks into the paving, its mask lifting to hover over the empty mark; at the same moment a newborn (0.08 tall, glowing warm white) steps out of one of the doors and grows to full height (0.25) during its 3-4 s walk to the vacancy, where the mask settles onto its face and the costume colour floods in. One death in four sets off a chain: a living actor leaves its mark for the vacancy, its mask flipping to the new role in mid-air, and the vacancy hops across 2-4 marks (traced by a brief gold thread between them) until a newborn fills the last gap. Now and then one actor carries three small masks orbiting its head (tyrant, benefactor, messenger). 2) The dialogue: between paired speakers small gold speech-beads arc back and forth at head height, one every 0.8-1.2 s, alternating direction; the stream never pauses, not even for a death, the beads simply landing on the hovering mask until the successor arrives. 3) The plot: a thin gold thread grows continuously from the well at about 0.3 units per second along a wandering 3D path that coils into an ever tighter knot around the star; whenever its tip comes within 1.5 units, a small dark obstacle-node appears and deflects it into another loop; the oldest segments fade so the knot stays legible (about 4000 points).
interactionDescription: Switches from a human lifetime to the city's own time. Off: actors live long enough that the scene seems changeless. On: time runs about 40x faster; births and deaths flicker through the cast so quickly that the bodies blur into pale ghost streaks, while the masks hang perfectly steady over their marks and the speech-beads fuse into continuous gold ribbons. Across the time-lapse the masks slowly shift in colour and shape, because the roles themselves drift, the plot-knot visibly thickens around its unreachable star, and the sky cycles through quick stage-lighting cues, one per act.
mood: Blue hour sliding into a theatrical evening. Deep violet-indigo overhead and a long rose afterglow low on the horizon; the square lit like a stage, warm gold from the footlights below and a cool moonlit key from above, so faces glow and shadows are long and thrown upward; lamps in a few windows; a thin plum haze softening the street vistas. Wry, ceremonial and a little melancholy: a comedy being watched by time.
caption: Step into Melania's square and you walk into the middle of a conversation: a soldier boasting, a father scolding his lovesick daughter, a servant hurrying past with a note. Return years later and the exchange has not paused, though every voice in it is new. The citizens are born into its parts and die out of them; masks pass from face to face like an inherited coat. Only the play grows older, edging toward an ending nobody lives to hear.
motto: The dialogue endures; only the voices are on loan.
camera: From the open south side, above the terraces, looking north across the stage into the central street vista: distance 34 from target (0, 2, -2), elevation 26 degrees, field of view 35. The footlights run along the lower third, the masked cast fills the middle, the horseshoe facades and receding streets form the backdrop, and the plot-knot with its star sits in the upper third.
